question: I'm planning a study where I'll use multiple regression with 5 predictors to predict patient outcomes. I want to be able to detect if these predictors together explain at least 10% of the variance in the outcome. How many subjects do I need for 80% power with alpha = 0.05? Use the omnibus Gaussian fixed-design F test with noncentrality N×R²/(1−R²), including an intercept.

I want to test whether a single biomarker predicts disease severity. If the biomarker explains about 15% of the variance in severity scores, how many patients do I need to detect this with 90% power at alpha = 0.05? Use the fixed-design Gaussian regression F test with one predictor and an intercept, and noncentrality N×R²/(1−R²).

I have a regression model with 4 predictors that explains 20% of the variance in patient recovery time. I want to test whether adding 3 new genetic markers improves the model to explain 30% of the variance. How many subjects do I need to detect this incremental improvement with 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Use the fixed-design Gaussian partial F test with residual degrees of freedom N−8 and noncentrality N×(R²_full−R²_reduced)/(1−R²_full).

We're building a prediction model with 10 predictors. We want to detect a medium effect size (Cohen's f² = 0.15) with 85% power at a more stringent alpha = 0.01. What sample size do we need? Use a fixed-design Gaussian omnibus F test of the 10 slopes with an intercept and noncentrality Nf².

In a Gaussian linear regression with eight predictors and an intercept, one predictor is the primary target. Its partial R², defined relative to the residual variance in the reduced model, is exactly 0.05. How many participants are required for 90% power at alpha = 0.05 using the fixed-design partial F test with noncentrality N×0.05/(1−0.05)?

We're conducting a large epidemiological study with 15 risk factors as predictors. We expect only a small effect (R² around 5%) since these are observational data. What sample size do we need for 95% power with alpha = 0.01? Use a fixed-design Gaussian omnibus F test of all slopes, with an intercept and noncentrality N×R²/(1−R²).

I'm analyzing whether a binary exposure (present in 50% of patients) predicts disease. The outcome rate is 20% in unexposed patients, and I expect an odds ratio of 2.0 for exposed vs unexposed. How many patients total for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Use a two-sided large-sample Wald test based on the information at the stated alternative, treating 50% as the planned exposure proportion.

In an equally allocated case-control study, exposure is normally distributed within each disease group, with a common SD. The difference in exposure means divided by this SD is log(1.5), so the retrospective design has an odds ratio of 1.5 per within-group SD. Use a logistic intercept and exposure coefficient, and the two-sided large-sample Wald test with information under this case-control sampling distribution. What minimum balanced total sample size gives 80% power at alpha = 0.05?

I'm building a multivariable logistic regression to predict readmission risk with 5 covariates. My main predictor is a continuous biomarker (normally distributed). I expect an odds ratio of 1.8 per SD increase in this biomarker, while adjusting for confounders that together explain about 10% of the variance in the predictor. Baseline readmission rate is 15%. How many patients for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Interpret the 15% as risk at the population mean biomarker value under the simple logistic planning model. Use the two-sided large-sample Wald information at the alternative and inflate the simple-logistic sample size before rounding by 1/(1−0.10) for covariate adjustment.

I'm studying a protective factor with an expected odds ratio of 0.6 (40% reduction in odds). The exposure is binary with 50% prevalence, and baseline disease rate in unexposed is 25%. What sample size do I need for 90% power at alpha = 0.05? Use a two-sided large-sample Wald test at the stated alternative and take the planned exposure proportion to be 0.50.

We're studying a rare outcome (5% baseline risk) and a binary exposure that's present in only 30% of the population. We expect an OR of 2.5 for exposed vs unexposed. What total sample size is needed for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? The 5% baseline risk applies to unexposed participants. Use the two-sided large-sample log-odds Wald test at the alternative, taking 30% as the anticipated rather than fixed exposure proportion.

I'm testing for an interaction between two binary risk factors in a logistic regression. Each factor has 50% prevalence and they're independent. Baseline risk (neither factor present) is 20%, main effect OR for each is 1.5, and the interaction OR is 2.0. What sample size do I need to detect this interaction with 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Fit both main effects and their interaction on the log-odds scale. Use the two-sided large-sample Wald test with alternative-model cell probabilities. Treat exposures as random with the stated probabilities; do not impose exact equal cell sizes.

I'm planning a longitudinal study with 4 repeated measures per subject, comparing treatment vs control. I expect a medium effect size (d = 0.5) between groups, and the ICC for within-subject correlation is about 0.5. How many subjects per group for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Assume a constant treatment difference across all visits, with d standardized by the single-visit marginal SD. Compare complete participant averages with a two-sided pooled t test assuming Gaussian outcomes and compound-symmetric within-person correlation.

We're doing a simple pre-post study comparing treatment vs control, with measurements at baseline and 8 weeks. We expect a treatment effect of d = 0.4, and within-patient correlation is about ICC = 0.6. How many subjects per group for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Define d using the marginal single-visit SD, common to baseline and follow-up. Compare independent Gaussian change scores using a two-sided pooled t test.

We're running a clinical trial with monthly visits over 6 months to detect a treatment effect of d = 0.35. The within-patient correlation (compound symmetry) is about ICC = 0.4. How many subjects per arm for 90% power at alpha = 0.05? Use exactly six postrandomization measurements, a constant treatment effect in marginal single-visit SD units, and a two-sided pooled t test of complete participant averages.

Our trial has patients nested within 10 clinics per treatment arm. The treatment effect is d = 0.3 and the ICC between patients within clinics is 0.05. How many patients per clinic do we need for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Randomization is by clinic. Assume equal clinic sizes, Gaussian outcomes with common marginal variance, and exchangeable within-clinic correlation. Analyze clinic means with a two-sided pooled t test with 18 degrees of freedom. Express d in units of the patient-level marginal SD.

We have a three-level study design: 3 measurements within patients, 15 patients within sites, and 5 sites per treatment arm. The variance is partitioned as: site variance = 0.02, patient variance = 0.50, residual = 0.48 (total = 1.0). We want to detect a treatment effect of d = 0.4. What power does this design achieve at alpha = 0.05? Randomize treatment at the site level and assume independent Gaussian site, patient and measurement effects. Compare site-level averages with a two-sided pooled t test with 8 degrees of freedom.

I'm analyzing a growth curve study comparing two groups over 8 time points (0-7). I expect the groups to differ in their slopes by 0.1 units per time point. The random intercept SD is 1.0, random slope SD is 0.3, and residual SD is 1.0. What's the minimum sample size per group to achieve 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Assume independent Gaussian errors with no serial correlation. Fit a separate ordinary least-squares slope to the eight observations of each participant, then compare individual slopes using a two-sided pooled t test.

I'm planning a 2-period AB/BA crossover trial. The within-subject correlation is 0.7, and the treatment effect is d = 0.6 (standardized by total SD). How many subjects do I need for 85% power at alpha = 0.05? Assume equal allocation to both sequences, common Gaussian outcome variance and a fixed period effect, with no carryover. Compare treatment-oriented paired differences with a period adjustment and N−2 residual degrees of freedom. Use a two-sided test.

I'm running a trial with 2 correlated outcomes (correlation = 0.6) measured at 3 time points. The treatment effect on the primary outcome is d = 0.4, and within-subject ICC is 0.5. I only need to power for the primary outcome (no multiplicity correction). How many subjects per group for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Assume a constant treatment effect on the primary outcome in single-visit marginal SD units and compound symmetry across visits. Use a two-sided pooled t test of the complete primary-outcome averages.

We're planning a survival trial where we expect the treatment to reduce the hazard by 30% (HR = 0.7). Control group median survival is 2 years. We'll have 3 years of accrual and 2 years of additional follow-up. How many patients per arm for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Assume 1:1 randomization, exponential hazards, uniform accrual and no loss to follow-up. Use the two-sided Schoenfeld event target and the mean arm-specific event yield, rounding up the per-arm sample size after conversion.

In our survival study, the control group has 50% 2-year survival and we expect HR = 0.65 for the treatment. With 2-year accrual and 1-year additional follow-up, how many patients per arm for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Assume 1:1 randomization, uniform accrual, exponential hazards and no loss to follow-up. Use the two-sided Schoenfeld event target and the mean arm-specific event yield without rounding the event target first.

I'm analyzing whether a continuous biomarker predicts survival. I expect an HR of 1.3 per standard deviation increase in the biomarker. About 25% of patients will experience the event during the study. How many patients for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Use the two-sided Schoenfeld approximation for a single biomarker, assuming unit variance in the risk sets. Divide the continuous event target by the event fraction before rounding the sample size.

We're planning a survival trial expecting HR = 0.75. Control 1-year survival is 70%. We'll have 18 months of accrual and 12 months of follow-up, but expect 20% dropout. How many patients per arm do we need for 85% power at alpha = 0.05, accounting for the dropout? Assume 1:1 randomization, exponential event hazards and uniform accrual. Model dropout for planning as a 20% proportional loss in the expected event yield. Use the two-sided Schoenfeld event target and round the resulting per-arm size up once.

We're planning a survival study to detect HR = 0.70 (treatment benefit). Control median survival is 18 months and total study duration is 36 months. With 1:1 allocation, 80% power, and alpha = 0.05, what's the total sample size needed across both arms? Assume exponential event hazards, 18 months of uniform accrual followed by 18 additional months, and no dropout. Use a two-sided Schoenfeld event target and round the implied equal arm sizes up.

We're studying a condition where about 30% of control patients are long-term survivors (essentially cured). We expect the treatment to increase this cure fraction to 45%. Among those who aren't cured, median survival is 2 years and we expect a modest HR of 0.8 for treatment vs control. With 5-year follow-up, how many per arm for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? The primary outcome is survival status at five years. In both arms, susceptible patients have exponential survival; cured patients survive past five years. Assume complete five-year ascertainment and equal allocation. Use the two-sided normal score planning approximation for comparing five-year survival probabilities at alpha = 0.05, with variances under the null and alternative and no continuity correction.

An equally allocated survival trial targets a cause-specific hazard ratio of 0.70 for a primary event. In the control arm, the cumulative incidences of the primary and competing events at a common fixed follow-up horizon are 0.30 and 0.15, respectively. Both cause-specific hazards are constant over time. Treatment leaves the competing cause-specific hazard unchanged. Everyone is observed until an event or the end of follow-up. Using the two-sided Schoenfeld event target and the mean arm-specific primary-event yield, what sample size per arm gives 80% power at alpha 0.05? Round up the arm size after conversion.

We're conducting a stratified survival analysis across 3 strata with different baseline hazards, but the treatment HR = 0.75 is assumed constant across strata. Over the 2-year study period, we expect 40% of controls to experience an event. What sample size per arm for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? The three strata are equally prevalent and have two-year control event probabilities of 0.04, 0.40 and 0.76. Assume equal allocation within each stratum, two years of complete follow-up, and proportional hazards within stratum. Use the two-sided Schoenfeld approximation for event count and the averaged event fraction across strata and arms. Round the overall per-arm size up. The stratum weights are planning proportions; equal enrollment quotas across strata are unnecessary.

We're comparing event rates between treatment and control. The control group has about 2 events per person-year, and we expect the treatment to increase this by 50% (rate ratio = 1.5). With 1-year follow-up, how many subjects per group for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Assume equal allocation and independent Poisson counts. Use an exact two-sided conditional rate test given the total count, allocating at most 0.025 to each tail.

We're testing whether a treatment reduces infection rate. Control patients average 0.5 infections per month, and we hope to reduce this to 0.3 per month. With 6 months of follow-up, how many per group for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Assume equal allocation and independent Poisson counts. Use an exact two-sided conditional rate test given the total count, allocating at most 0.025 to each tail.

Our outcome is count data with overdispersion (variance greater than mean). The control group averages 5 events, treatment group expected to average 4 events, with dispersion parameter k = 2. How many per group for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Assume independent negative binomial counts with Var(Y)=μ+μ²/k and common size k=2. Use equal allocation and a two-sided large-sample log mean ratio Wald test with variance under the alternative.

We're analyzing count data where patients have variable follow-up time (mean 0.8 years, SD 0.3 years). The baseline event rate is 3 per year, and we want to detect a rate ratio of 1.4. How many subjects per group for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Assume independent, noninformative follow-up and a correctly specified conditional Poisson model with a log-exposure offset. Use equal allocation, expected information at the alternative and a two-sided log rate ratio Wald test.

Our count outcome has 30% structural zeros (patients who can never experience the event). Among those who can have events, the control mean is 3 and treatment mean is 2. What sample size per group for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Assume independent zero-inflated Poisson counts with equal allocation. Compare the Poisson component means using a two-sided large-sample Wald test for the log rate ratio, estimating the structural-zero proportion separately in each arm. Use expected information at the planning values.

I'm studying a condition where the event rate increases by about 10% each year. At baseline (time 0), the rate is 1 event per person-year. I want to detect if a treatment reduces the rate ratio to 0.8 over a 3-year follow-up period. What sample size per group for 80% power at alpha = 0.05? Assume the control rate is constant in each year and multiplies by 1.10 at the start of each new year, with the same treatment rate ratio throughout. Follow everyone for all three years. Use equal allocation and a two-sided Poisson log rate ratio Wald planning approximation.

We have 20 clinics per arm with 25 subjects per clinic. The ICC is 0.03, baseline rate is 4 events per person-year, and we want to detect a rate ratio of 1.25. What power does this cluster design achieve at alpha = 0.05? Each participant is followed for one year. Use a count-scale design effect 1+(25−1)×0.03 for log rate-ratio variance and approximate power by the two-sided noncentral t distribution with 38 degrees of freedom.
